name: Uma Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, unions, AI firms or government. Your answers stay confidential. What is a normal workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Uma Tanaka, 58, and I've built and repaired power lines since my certificate and apprenticeship. I know how wet soil moves a pole near Orchard Bend, though I'm paid at the lower end of the trade; I enjoy training a new hand, and I still check uncertain work with the crew lead.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is on your mind outside work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A roof leak used almost all our savings. My partner Arun drives a community bus on hours that change with local events, and our grown children have their own homes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a faster work ticket is fine after a fault, but it won't show whether a pole has shifted in wet soil. We still need a person to look and test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, nothing changing much would still leave us counting money. My line pay is low, we used our savings on a leaking roof, and Arun's community-bus hours fall when local events stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep taking my normal repair rota and ask for the safe weekend callouts that fit our bus schedule. In the first year we'd stop buying the ready-made meals we keep for late shifts until the roof balance is cleared; I might use the approved AI note helper occasionally after the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel capable on a line and anxious over the roof bill. Our grown children are settled elsewhere, so we aren't buying school things, but we do have the house to keep dry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What made you spot a shifted pole?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The post by Orchard Bend had fresh mud on one side and a different lean after rain. We measured before tightening the service wire, and the crew lead agreed it needed a new support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you used the note helper before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A couple of times, after another worker showed me where the circuit number goes. I still read the signed sheet before I send the record.

say: I'd accept **faster tickets** after a field repair.
I'd insist on **wet-ground checks** before anyone trusts the drawing.
think: Our **roof leak** emptied savings while my line pay remains low.
Arun's **event-dependent bus hours** make household money change from month to month.
do: Take **normal repairs** and ask for safe weekend callouts that fit the bus rota.
Stop buying **ready-made meals** until the roof balance clears; use approved AI notes only after repairs.
feel: **Capable** at work and anxious about the roof bill.
S0.quote: We measured before tightening the service wire, and the crew lead agreed it needed a new support.
fieldNote: Uma's **field judgement** is visible in a rain-shifted Orchard Bend pole, though she still checks with the crew lead.
The **roof cost** and Arun's variable bus hours keep her anxious even when AI adds little.

steps.text: Take normal line repairs and safe weekend callouts
Stop buying ready-made meals until the roof balance clears

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the depot to test new buying and route software with the crews who use the parts. A missing pole brace costs us more time than a slow purchase order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my field work lasts while robots spread slowly, but better scheduling could take some weekend callouts. Arun's bus work is hands-on and should last for now, so we'd be managing one reduced pay stream rather than two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the storekeeper to show me the approved stock tool after the crew has run it through a winter month. In the first year I'd compare its brace counts with the truck bins, keep taking line shifts and put off repainting our kitchen if my callout pay falls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel watchful, not hostile to the tool. I can learn it after others prove it. A wrong count in a snow call wastes the whole morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What brace count went wrong recently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We once had three braces listed and only two on the truck. I drove back for the third, so I'd want the new system to count actual bins, not just yesterday's order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does repainting matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The walls are stained but sound. Arun and I can wait another season if the overtime that pays for paint doesn't come.

say: I'd demand **winter stock trials** before the new buying system is trusted.
I'd say **correct brace counts** matter more than fast orders.
think: My **weekend callouts** could shrink as scheduling improves.
Arun's **bus wages** look safer for now because hands-on robots spread slowly.
do: Learn the **approved stock tool** after a crew-tested winter month.
Compare **brace bins** with screen counts and delay kitchen paint if callout pay falls.
feel: **Watchful**, willing to adopt a proven tool.
S1.quote: A wrong count in a snow call wastes the whole morning.
fieldNote: Uma expects **field work to continue** but sees real risk to the weekend overtime that funds household improvements.
Her **stock adoption** requires a winter crew test and a physical bin count, matching her steady approach to new tools.

steps.text: Learn the approved stock tool after the winter crew trial
Delay buying kitchen paint if weekend callout pay falls
Continue paid line shifts and compare brace bins with screen counts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the depot thinking AI in 2028 may change orders and plans, but robots around 2031 are what could climb and repair. Employers should offer paid apprenticeships for testing those machines before they cut crews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 63 when capable repair robots arrive, and I could lose much of my line pay. Arun's bus driving might face the same machines; less than a month is saved and there are only a few utility jobs near us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the company for its robot test timetable and the training office about a paid equipment-testing apprenticeship. In 2029 I'd enroll if wages continue; during the first robot year I'd apply for posted testing work and ask our grown daughter to check bus routes to employers beyond town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel frightened about two physical jobs changing together, but I can still make a plan. I wouldn't leave a paid shift for a course that offers only a certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask your daughter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My grown daughter can help compare bus timetables and interview times, not pay our bills. Her own children need her income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What test would matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The Orchard Bend pole shifted after rain, so a robot should notice ground movement before tightening a wire. I'd want that in the trial record, not a sales video.

say: I'd separate **2028 planning AI** from 2031 repair robots.
I'd ask for **paid testing apprenticeships** before line crews shrink.
think: At **63**, I may lose much of my line pay.
Arun's **bus income** could also face robots while our savings cover less than a month.
do: Request the **robot test timetable** and paid apprenticeship details now.
Enroll if **wages continue** in 2029; apply for posted testing work in 2031.
feel: **Frightened** about two wages, with a conditional training plan.
S2.quote: I wouldn't leave a paid shift for a course that offers only a certificate.
fieldNote: Uma sees **2031 robots** as a threat to both line repairs and Arun's driving, unlike the earlier planning change.
Her **apprenticeship condition** is continued pay; family help is limited to travel information, not a substitute income.

steps.text: Request the company robot testing timetable before changing jobs
Enroll in equipment-testing training in 2029 if wages continue
Apply for posted testing roles when robots arrive in 2031
Ask her grown daughter to compare travel routes to regional interviews

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to trial robots on wet ground and tell workers what a paid new job would involve. Thinking AI arrives in 2031, and field robots around 2034, when I'll be 66.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 66 retirement might be possible, but our roof debt and thin reserve make it uncertain. Arun may also lose bus shifts when capable robots spread, so I want figures for both of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd request both retirement statements and ask the crew lead to include Orchard Bend in a robot field trial. In 2032 I'd take a paid inspection placement if offered; in 2034 I'd compare our low-income budget with a posted inspection wage before choosing retirement or work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel less rushed, though the bill still presses. Five years gives us time to check the soil, the machine and the actual retirement figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the low-income budget include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Roof repayment, fuel and medicines, with a low figure for Arun's bus shifts. We wouldn't use his busiest festival month as a promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there is no placement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep safe line shifts while the utility offers them and ask local employers what a real inspection post pays. There aren't many, so I need names and wages, not an idea.

say: I'd ask for **wet-ground robot trials** and clear paid job terms.
I'd distinguish **2031 thinking AI** from 2034 field robots.
think: Retirement at **66** needs figures for both partners.
Our **roof debt** and Arun's possible bus-hour loss make the decision tight.
do: Request **both retirement statements** and propose Orchard Bend for testing.
Take a **paid placement** if offered in 2032; compare a posted wage with retirement in 2034.
feel: **Less rushed**, still pressed by roof costs.
S3.quote: I need names and wages, not an idea.
fieldNote: Uma's **2034 decision** depends on verified income and a low case for Arun's bus hours, not age alone.
Her **robot trial proposal** uses an actual ground movement hazard, while paid inspection work remains a posted possibility.

steps.text: Compare written retirement figures with roof debt and low bus income
Take a paid inspection placement in 2032 if offered
Keep safe paid line shifts if no placement opens
Apply for posted inspection work if retirement income falls short

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell apprentices to learn why a pole moved, not merely read the point on a screen. Thinking AI arrives in 2036, and field robots around 2039, when I'll be 71.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might have retired before 71 if we clear the roof debt and our written figures cover us. Arun's bus work could change before then, so I can't treat his current hours as fixed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep paid repair shifts and clear the roof balance, then request updated retirement figures each year. In 2037 Arun and I would choose a date only if a low-income budget covers our bills; by 2039 I'd leave the Orchard Bend ground notes with the next apprentice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calmer about the distant robot and still anxious about the next roof payment. A decade is useful if we keep working and actually reduce the balance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you save while paying the roof bill?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: After the balance is clear, I'd put ten from each real weekend callout into savings. I can't count callouts the utility hasn't assigned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is in the ground notes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rain date, the pole lean and the measurement before we moved the anchor. An apprentice can compare those with the soil under their own boots.

say: I'd tell apprentices to learn **ground movement** through real measurements.
I'd name **2039 field robots** as the hands-on change when I'll be 71.
think: Retirement before **71** depends on clearing roof debt and verified income.
Arun's **bus shifts** could change, so current hours cannot anchor the plan.
do: Keep **paid repairs**, clear roof debt and request annual retirement figures.
Save **ten from real callouts** after debt clears, then choose a date only if bills fit.
feel: **Calmer** about robots, anxious about the next roof payment.
S4.quote: An apprentice can compare those with the soil under their own boots.
fieldNote: Uma's **long runway** reduces immediate robot pressure but leaves an active roof repayment and uncertain bus hours.
Her **conditional saving** starts after debt clearance, and her field notes preserve measured ground movement for apprentices.

steps.text: Continue paid repairs and clear the roof balance
Save ten from each actual weekend callout after roof debt clears
Choose a 2037 retirement date only if low-income figures cover bills

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because 2031 robots could reach both my line repairs and Arun's bus driving. Paid equipment training, a real test schedule, posted jobs and travel information would help me keep earning.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether a machine notices ground that moved overnight in rain. A clean drawing can't feel the mud under a pole.

headlineQuote: A clean drawing can't feel the mud under a pole.
portrait: Uma is a **58-year-old experienced lineworker** with a certificate and apprenticeship, low pay and less than one month saved.
A **roof leak** drained savings while Arun's event-based bus hours make their income uneven.
She uses **AI occasionally** for finished notes after coworkers show the approved system, while field measurements govern safety.
The **2031 robot date** worries her because both physical jobs could lose hours with few local utility openings.
Longer warning supports **roof repayment**, plus a measured ground record for future apprentices.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries Uma most because 2031 robots could affect both her line work and Arun's bus wages.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **paid equipment training**, real trials, posted jobs and help planning travel to interviews.
